script:
These robots are learning how to walk before they even exist.
What you're looking at is thousands of virtual robots training inside a physics simulator.
See, walking on legs is basically controlled falling.
Instead of hand-tuning every step, engineers let them learn by trial and error, like a video game.
Every time one falls, it resets and tries again, earning rewards for staying upright.
And the crazy part is the speed.
With thousands of clones running on GPUs, a four-legged robot learns to walk in minutes.
Humanoids like Figure 02 pack years of walking into a few hours.
Of course, there's one big catch.
Real motors lag, sensors are noisy, and every floor has different grip.
So a robot trained in a perfect simulation fails immediately on real hardware.
Here's the wildest part.
Engineers intentionally make the simulation chaotic.
They randomize friction and weight, and constantly shove the robots.
Survive that, and you drop the AI brain onto a real robot and it just walks.
In a few years, almost every skill a robot learns will happen in simulation first.
Follow for more stories on tech, AI, and robotics.

sources.supports: Thousands of simulated robots training in parallel on a GPU, resetting when they fall, earning rewards during training, a four-legged robot (ANYmal) learning to walk in minutes, and randomizing ground friction and pushing robots in simulation for sim-to-real transfer

Figure 02 humanoid robots training through trial and error in a GPU-accelerated physics simulator with thousands of virtual robots in parallel, compressing years of walking data into a few hours, randomizing physical properties, friction, and shoves, and transferring policies zero-shot to physical robots

Walking on legs described as controlled falling, shifting from hand-tuned controllers to reinforcement learning with upright rewards, policies trained in a perfect simulation failing immediately on real hardware, floors differing in grip, domain randomization varying mass distribution, friction, and shoves, and policies dropping onto real hardware and working
Real-world motor communication latency (lag), sensor noise, and friction differences creating the sim-to-real gap between physics simulators and physical hardware
